1:
The place-name is a puzzle before it is a location. Gill explains Ramathaim as a dual, two Ramahs, the city consisting of two parts built perhaps on two hills, and offers three accounts of the addition Zophim: that the Rabbins take the hills to have looked one at another; that being on eminences they had watchtowers with watchmen set in them; or that the word means prophets, who are sometimes called watchmen, so that a school of the prophets stood here — a reading the Targum seems to countenance, since it renders the opening clause there was one man of Ramatha, of the disciples of the prophets. He records from Jerome that this is the Arimathaea of Joseph, in the Thamnitic region near Lydda. Ellicott runs through the same list and then chooses: the prophet-watchmen derivation is interesting though fanciful, and the simplest and least strained explanation refers the name to hills so placed that they watched one another, or better still to watch-towers built at an early date on the two summits. Henry is blunter still about the school. Prophecy, he thinks, revived in Samuel; before his time there was for a great while no open vision, and from Moses to Samuel scarcely a prophet of the Lord is so much as mentioned, so that we have no reason to think there was any nursery or college of prophets at Ramah until Samuel himself founded one there.

Elkanah's descent raises the second difficulty, since the verse makes him an Ephrathite and the genealogy in Chronicles makes him a Levite. Henry takes Ephrathite in the older sense: his ancestor Zuph was of Bethlehem-Judah, which was called Ephrathah, where this family of the Levites was first seated before one branch of it removed to Mount Ephraim — and perhaps the notice of their being originally Ephrathites is given to show their alliance to David. Wesley says the same in a line, that Elkanah was of Bethlehem-Judah by birth and habitation though by his original a Levite. Ellicott takes the word the other way, as meaning Ephraimite, and explains it by civil standing rather than by tribe: a Levite of the family of Kohath, he belonged for civil purposes to the tribe among whom he lived. He then answers a difficulty others have raised, that a Levite's son needed no dedication such as Hannah made — the Levitical service began only at twenty-five and even then was not continuous, whereas the dedication of Samuel was life-long.

The verse also opens a book, and the commentators differ over how much its first word carries. Clarke reads it as a joint: these books were formerly reckoned the four books of Kings, the two of Samuel anciently made but one, and the separation seems to have been done without reason or necessity; properly speaking they are a continuation of the book of Judges. Ellicott denies the inference. The introductory words do not signify that this history continues Judges or any preceding writing; it is a common historical formula, standing at the head of Joshua, Ruth, Esther, Ezra and Ezekiel alike. Keil is concerned with the division rather than the join: the books originally formed one undivided work, and in the Hebrew manuscripts they do so still, the split into two having originated with the Alexandrian translators and reaching the printed Hebrew Bible only in the sixteenth century. He notes that the Greek calls them books of the kingdoms, a title he allows so far as each of the two works gives the history of a double kingdom — here Saul's and David's. Clarke reports the tradition of authorship without endorsing it: the Hebrew copies carry Samuel's name as a running title, though it was not anciently prefixed, and the Jews commonly hold that he wrote the first twenty-seven chapters and Gad and Nathan the last four.
2:
Every voice here treats the two wives as the wound the chapter is written to show. Gill says the practice was connived at in those times but was contrary to the original law of marriage, and that Elkanah, though a good man, was chastised for it with a great deal of vexation and trouble, his two wives never agreeing; Wesley agrees it was a transgression of the original institution, and both guess that he took Peninnah because Hannah was barren. Clarke states the rule from experience: the custom of those times permitted it, but wherever there was more than one wife we find the peace of the family greatly disturbed. Ellicott sets it in a longer frame. The primeval divine ordination sanctioned monogamy alone, and in the Mosaic code polygamy is accepted as a custom everywhere prevailing but never approved, the laws seeking, as with slavery, only to restrict and limit it. The writer here, he thinks, quietly shows up the curse which almost invariably attended this miserable violation of the home, one of the many gently-worded but fire-tipped rebukes the Old Testament directs at sins condoned and even approved by the voice of mankind.

On the yearly journey the voices differ over which feast is meant. Gill takes it from solemn feast to solemn feast, there being three in the year at which every male appeared. Wesley adds that as a Levite he went at other times too in his course. Ellicott narrows it: the Hebrew word rendered yearly is the one used of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and there is little doubt that the Passover is meant. All of them stop at the divine title. Clarke observes that this is the first place in the Bible where the Lord of hosts is found, and takes the hosts for the heavenly bodies, so that to call Jehovah their Lord was to declare him their Maker and Governor and therefore the proper object of worship rather than they — the superiority of Israel's religion to all that heathenism could boast. Ellicott counts the title some two hundred and sixty times in the Old Testament and none of it in the books compiled before this one, and finds it significant that it should first appear in the books which tell of the setting up of an earthly throne, as the protest of Samuel and his school against any eclipsing of the invisible sovereignty by the passing splendours of a monarchy.

The portion given to Hannah is the chapter's hardest phrase. Gill reports the Targum's one choice portion, the best part of the peace offering left after the priest's share, and notes that the word is dual, so that some render it a double portion and others one part of two faces. Clarke calls the Hebrew very obscure and lays the versions side by side — the Syriac has double, the Chaldee chosen, the Vulgate that he being sorrowful gave her one part. Keil and Ellicott settle on one portion for two persons, a double share, and read it as a sign, in Von Gerlach's words, that thou art as dear to me as if thou hadst borne me a child; Ellicott grants that the Vulgate, Luther and Abarbanel favour the reading that turns the husband unkind, but holds the double portion preferable both grammatically and exegetically. Gill says the rival upbraided her with her barrenness continually, and Ellicott that the one sin poisons a household otherwise quiet and Godfearing, Peninnah choosing the solemn occasion of the thank-offering to refer her rival's childlessness to the special anger of God. Of the husband's question Keil says only that ten is a round number for many, while Clarke turns it into its own answer — is not his especial affection better than all the comfort a numerous family could give?
9:
Henry finds the gentle reproof already working. It brought her to her meat: she did not harden herself in sorrow, nor grow sullen when she was reproved for it, but perceiving her husband uneasy that she would not come and eat with them, she cheered up her own spirits as well as she could and came to table. Gill reads the clause of the whole party, who had eaten heartily and drunk freely and made a feast of it where the tabernacle and altar were; but he notes that the Targum makes it after SHE had eaten and drunk, on the ground that her husband's entreaty may have prevailed on her to eat somewhat, though little, and to drink, though it were but water, since she afterwards declares she had touched neither wine nor strong drink. Ellicott calls it simply the solemn sacrificial meal at which the whole family were present; Keil marks the rising as the turn of the story, Hannah getting up with a troubled heart when the meal was over to pour out her grief in prayer before God.

The second half of the verse raises two questions the voices answer differently. On the seat, Clarke says it was the throne of judgment, since Eli was then judge of Israel; Wesley grants it was manifestly raised higher than ordinary but thinks he sat there rather as high priest, to hear and answer such as came to him for advice and to inspect and direct the worship of God; Ellicott takes it as both at once, a chair or throne of state where the high-priestly judge sat at certain times to administer justice. He adds that Eli was of the line of Ithamar, the younger son of Aaron, though what moved the dignity across from the elder line of Eleazar is lost. On the word temple the three separate further. Clarke thinks this the first place where the temple of Jehovah is named at all, which gives room for a strong suspicion that these books were not compiled until the first temple was built, or later still. Wesley answers in a line that it means the tabernacle, which is frequently so called. Ellicott takes a middle way: the Hebrew word rendered post, and the later mention of the doors of the house, seem to suggest that a permanent home had by now been raised for the sanctuary, something of a building, possibly of stone, surrounding the tabernacle; and he would render the phrase palace of the Lord, so called not from any external magnificence but as the earthly place where at times the visible glory of Israel's King was pleased to manifest itself.

Henry follows the movement from the table to the prayer, and makes the reasoning her own. It put her upon considering: do I well to be angry, do I well to fret, what good does it do me? Had I not better ease myself of it, and cast it upon the Lord by prayer? Her husband's question, whether he were not better to her than ten sons, may have set the thought going — whether he be so or no, God is, and therefore to him will I apply, and before him will I pour out my complaint. The moment, he adds, was as well chosen as the place. They were at the door of the tabernacle, where God had promised to meet his people; they had lately offered their peace-offerings and, taking the comfort of being accepted, had feasted upon the sacrifice; and now it was proper to put up her prayer in virtue of that sacrifice, since by a peace-offering not only is atonement made for sin, but the audience and acceptance of our prayers is obtained. To that sacrifice, in all our supplications, we must have an eye.
10:
Ellicott counts two promises in the vow. The first pledged the son she prayed for to the service of the Eternal all the days of his life — though the mother looked only to a life-long service in the ritual of the Tabernacle, and the Being who heard her destined him for higher work, the priestly duties soon merging in the far more responsible ones of the prophet and reformer of the people. The second undertook that he should be a Nazarite, which included three things: refraining from intoxicating drink, letting the hair grow, and avoiding all ceremonial defilement by corpses even of the nearest kin. Samuel was what the Talmud calls a perpetual Nazarite, and the untouched hair singled out here was a public protest that he had renounced intercourse with the world and devoted the whole fulness of life to the Lord's work. Clarke marks how much the vow added to what was owed already: as a descendant of Levi the boy was the Lord's property from twenty-five years of age to fifty, but this pledged him from infancy to death and made him not a Levite only but a Nazarite. Wesley says it in six words, a perpetual Nazarite. Gill raises the legal question the others pass by: a woman's vow was void if her husband disapproved, and Jewish tradition holds that a man may vow his son a Nazarite but a woman may not — a tradition this verse contradicts, which is why, he says, they labour to explain the vow away.

How she prayed is the next thing noticed. Gill takes the phrase to mean she was earnest and importunate, repeating her petition and prolonging her prayer, unwilling to let the Lord go until she had some satisfaction that she should have what she asked; some think she continued an hour. Wesley reads the Hebrew as multiplied to pray, and draws a rule from it: she plainly said much more than is here expressed, and the like is to be judged of the prayers and sermons of other holy persons in scripture, which give us only the sum and substance of them. That the prayer was silent all agree. Gill calls it mental prayer, ejaculations of her mind which she knew were well known to God without being expressed vocally; Clarke says her whole heart was engaged, and though she spake not with an audible voice her lips formed themselves according to the pronunciation of the words her heart uttered; Keil renders the idiom speaking to her heart.

Why the high priest read it as drunkenness the voices answer three ways. Keil keeps to what the verse says: he noticed her mouth, saw the lips move without a voice, and told her to put away her wine — that is, go away and sleep off her intoxication. Gill supposes a longer history behind the rebuke, since the words sound like what, every day drunk, continually in this wicked practice, so that Eli may have observed odd looks and a strange behaviour in her at other times which he had put down to wine; the Targum has him ask instead how long she will behave like a fool or a mad woman. Wesley points at the scene itself, the multitude of her words and those motions of her face and body which the vehemency of her passion and her fervency in prayer occasioned. Ellicott, following Bunsen, turns the charge back on the sanctuary: Eli was struck with dismay at her silent earnestness, such heartfelt prayer being apparently not usual at that time, and remembering the state of the moral life in the precincts over which he ruled with so weak and vacillating a rule, and how sadly frequent disorders were at the sacrificial meal, he at once suspected that the weeping woman was drunk — though he quickly atoned for the unworthy suspicion.
15:
How the two words no, my lord are to be heard is itself in dispute. Gill takes them as spoken with great mildness and meekness, without falling into a passion at so scandalous an imputation, and with the respect due to Eli's office. Ellicott quotes Calvin for the same reading, that we should consider the modesty of Hannah, who though she had received injury from the high priest yet answers with reverence and humility. But both men record the other tradition, which hears an edge in the phrase: some in the Talmud understood her to mean that he was no lord in this matter, and that the Holy Spirit did not rest upon him, or he would never have suspected her — which, Gill adds, he had sufficiently shown by suspecting her at all. Clarke keeps to the vindication itself and admires its construction: neither wine nor inebriating drink has been poured out unto me, but I have poured out my soul unto the Lord, which he calls a great deal of delicacy and point.

What she asks Eli not to think of her is read two ways. Gill takes daughter of Belial in the ordinary sense of a yokeless, lawless, impudent and abandoned creature, one of the vilest of wretches, as she must be who came drunk into the sanctuary of God; and he adds that drunkenness is an abominable crime in a man but much more in a woman, the Romans having made it in them a capital offence. Clarke construes the Hebrew differently, as put not thy handmaid before the faces of a daughter of Belial — that is, expose me not to reproach before such women, several of whom probably attended at the sanctuary for the purposes of prostitution and gain, since we read soon after that the sons of Eli lay with the women at the door of the tabernacle. He draws the obvious conclusion from both halves of the scene: that the high priest could suppose a praying woman drunk, and that such women were to be found there at all, proves religion was at a very low ebb in Shiloh.

Eli's answer is short and the commentators weigh it carefully. Keil insists it was not a prediction but a pious wish, which God in his grace most gloriously fulfilled. Gill notes what changed the old man's mind, that her discourse was not only sober and rational but religious and spiritual, so that he dismissed her in peace and bade her not distress herself with what he had said. Ellicott makes the moment a window on the whole character. Weak and over-indulgent to his headstrong wicked sons, probably too self-indulgent and a lover of ease, Eli yet shows flashes of true nobility, real generosity and self-forgetfulness which light up a life that closed in failure and disaster; here he is quick to see that he has been insulting a blameless woman, retracts the cruel accusation at once, accuses himself of precipitancy in his courteous farewell, and in his fatherly wish almost promises her what she had asked. Of her leaving, Keil says she was strengthened and comforted by the word of the high priest, which assured her that her prayer would be heard, and that the text leaves the reader to supply the missing word — her countenance was no more troubled, as it had been. Wesley traces the change further back, to God's Spirit setting the priest's words home upon her and assuring her that both his prayers and hers should be heard. Ellicott calls it a beautiful example of the composing influence of prayer: she had cast her burden upon the Lord, so her own spirit was relieved of its load, and she returned to the feast and ate her portion with a cheerful heart.
19:
Gill gives the plain reason for the early rising, partly devotion and partly the journey, but Henry will not let the detail go so quickly. Observe, he says, how they improved their time at the tabernacle: every day they were there, even the day fixed for going home, they worshipped God, and rose early to do it. It is good to begin the day with God; let him that is the first have the first. They had a journey before them and a family of children to take with them, and yet they would not stir till they had worshipped God together — prayer and provender do not hinder a journey. They had already spent several days in religious worship and yet they attended once more, for we should not be weary of well-doing. Ellicott reads the same verse as another notice of the pious customs of this household, and a striking picture of one of the many holy homes that existed in Israel even in the wild, disorderly days of the Judges, standing against the deep degradation of the priests at the sanctuary; and he notes in passing that the house at Ramah uses the short familiar name of the town the first verse called the Ramahs of the Watchers.

Then comes the turn of the whole story in three words. Keil states the sequence flatly: they worshipped, Elkanah returned home to Ramah with his two wives, he knew his wife Hannah, and Jehovah remembered her — that is, heard her prayer. Wesley glosses the verb by its effect, that God manifested his remembrance of her by what followed. Henry takes it as the answer to the exact thing she had asked, since the Lord remembered Hannah, which was the very thing she desired, and more she needed not desire; and he draws the general comfort out of it, that though God seem long to forget his people's burdens and troubles and cares and prayers, he will at length make it appear that they are not out of his mind.

The name the child was given is argued over as closely as anything in the chapter. Henry reports two accounts and will not choose between them: some make its etymology much the same with that of Ishmael, heard of God, because the mother's prayers were remarkably heard and he was an answer to them; others, taking their cue from the reason she herself gives, make it mean asked of God — and it comes nearly to the same thing, since by either she designed to perpetuate the remembrance of God's favour in answering her, so that at every mention of his name she might take the comfort to herself and give God the glory. Keil is stricter. The name is not formed from the word for name together with the name of God, as one respected lexicon had it, but from a compound meaning heard of God; and the clause because I have asked him of the Lord is not an etymological explanation of the name at all, but an exposition founded upon the facts. Henry lets the practical weight fall where the mother meant it to: mercies given in answer to prayer are to be remembered with peculiar expressions of thankfulness, and how many seasonable deliverances and supplies might we call Samuels, asked of God — whatever is so we are in a special manner engaged to devote to him. She intended the name to put her son in mind of the obligation he was under to be the Lord's, having been asked of God and dedicated to him at once; for a child of prayer is in a special manner bound to be a good child.
20:
Gill weighs the phrase that dates the birth. At the revolutions of days may mean a complete year from their return home, as Ben Melech took it, though he thinks the sense rather the nine months of a woman's going with child. Clarke, coming at the name from the reason the mother gives, holds that the Hebrew must be considerably contracted if it is to carry that sense, its components being the words for asked of God — a name to keep both mother and son in continual remembrance of the divine interposition at his birth. The next verse then lets slip something the narrative had not told us. Keil points out that the words and his vow show Elkanah to have vowed a vow of his own, in case his beloved Hannah should have a son, and that his vow concerned the presentation of a sacrifice, which is why it stands coupled with the yearly offering. Wesley draws the further inference: though it was nowhere said before, it now appears that the husband had heard his wife's vow and consented to it, and had added a vow of his own if God answered their prayers.

Hannah alone stays behind, and the commentators explain both the liberty and the reason. Gill notes that women might go to the yearly feasts if they pleased but were not obliged to, and leaves open whether she went up at the time appointed for her purification and for the redeeming of a firstborn, since the Scriptures do not relate every fact that was done, though what follows looks rather as if she did not. Clarke states her purpose simply, that she would not go up to Shiloh till her son was old enough to be employed in the divine service. Ellicott fixes how long that would be: weaning took place very late among the Hebrews, and it appears from the books of the Maccabees that mothers were in the habit of suckling their children for three years. Wesley stretches the word further still. Weaned means not only from the breast but from the mother's knee and care and from childish food, until the child was something grown and fit to do some service in the tabernacle — for as soon as he was brought up he worshipped God, and presently after was ministering to Eli.

Elkanah's consent is generous and Gill hears it as such, a kind and indulgent husband speaking, who knew she would break no law of God by staying and saw that the delay might be better for her health and the child's. What he adds is harder. The prayer that the Lord would establish his word points to a word nowhere recorded, and each voice supplies it differently. Keil rejects the Rabbinic view that some direct revelation had been made about Samuel's birth and destination, and takes the word to be Eli's — the God of Israel grant thy petition — which the parents might well regard after the birth as a promise from Jehovah himself, and might naturally pray to see carried through. Ellicott records the tradition Keil dismisses, in the form Rashi gives it: a voice from heaven went forth saying that there should arise a just one whose name should be Samuel, whereupon every mother who bore a son called him Samuel and, seeing his actions, said this was not he; but when this one was born they said, this is that Samuel. If the tradition is declined, he offers Bunsen's plainer sense, that the Lord would fulfil what he designs with the child and has promised by his birth. Wesley turns the word back on the vow itself, the matter concerning the child which she had vowed. Clarke turns it into a father's prayer — that the Lord would preserve the child, cause him to grow up, and make him a blessing to Israel.
24:
What Hannah brought with the child is disputed at the first word. Clarke prefers the reading of the Greek, Syriac and Arabic, a bullock of three years old rather than three bullocks, and argues it from the next verse, where they slay THE bullock and no more are heard of, a beast of that age being the one ordinarily used. Wesley keeps the three and assigns them, one for a burnt-offering, the second for a sin-offering, the third for a peace-offering; when the next verse speaks of one he takes it for the singular put for the plural, which is frequent. Keil keeps the three too and explains the singular differently, as pointing to the particular sacrifice that went with the presentation — the burnt-offering by which the boy was consecrated to a lifelong service at the sanctuary — the other two being brought for another use. Gill leaves all these open, and adds that the beast slain may have been a present to Eli at the boy's introduction to him. Of the rest of the gift Clarke notes that the bottle was a skin, their vessels for wine being made of goat skins stripped off whole and sewn up.

Gill hears the mother's opening words through the Targum, which makes them a request rather than an address — I beseech thee, my lord — that Eli would look upon her son, take him under his care as a scholar to be instructed in the law, and enter him into his service; and he supposes Eli might well be backward to it, a Levite not being admitted to service before twenty-five. Ellicott stops instead at the form of her oath. As thy soul liveth is peculiar to these books, occurring six times here and only once in Kings, which accords with the age of the Judges and of Saul being characteristically the age of vows. Keil describes what the words did: at the presentation of the boy his mother made herself known to the high priest as the woman who had prayed to the Lord in that very place.

The last claim she makes on the child is the hardest phrase in the chapter, and the voices split three ways over the rendering. Clarke defends the received translation on grammatical ground: the root means he asked, and in one of its conjugations the verb signifies to lend — a double sense the Vulgate, Septuagint and Syriac all follow, so that lent him to the Lord answers to the asked of him two verses earlier. Ellicott calls the rendering flatly false and would have it, therefore I also make him one asked of the Lord, all the days that he liveth he is asked of the Lord, the sense being that the Lord gave him to her, and she now returns him whom she obtained by prayer. Keil is of the same mind and traces the error, saying that the meaning to lend which the lexicons give has no support but a false rendering in the Greek, and that Jehovah had not lent the son to Hannah at all. Wesley keeps the word and turns it into comfort: she lent him, but not with any purpose of requiring him again, and whatever we give to God may in that sense be said to be lent to him, since though we may not recall it he will certainly repay it to our unspeakable advantage. Even the last clause is contested. Clarke reports manuscripts and versions reading and they worshipped, and thinks everything from her address to the end of the song is likely Hannah's own, so that the clause should read and she worshipped there. Wesley and Ellicott both take it of the boy — not Eli but young Samuel, who could worship in some sort, at least with outward adoration, putting his own child-seal to his mother's gift of him.
